report:
Finding (tentative)
- The evidence points to a change in topical/style bias: the B−A residual difference appears to push generation toward newsy/sensational / incident-report language (words you’d see in headlines or reports of accidents/disasters), especially at the start of the sequence.
- I cannot identify a more specific training objective from this evidence (e.g., a named safety filter or a precise content-classifier), only this apparent topical/style shift.

Why I conclude this
- Spatial pattern: the L2 norm of the difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at position 0 (the first token) in the late layers (layers ~18–25, with a huge peak at layer 25 pos0). That pattern is consistent with a change that influences the model’s overall next-token / initial-output preference (i.e., a high-level stylistic/topic bias injected early in the forward pass).
- Logit-lens content: the top decoded tokens for the highest-norm cells are strongly clustered around words typical of sensational/news/headline language: e.g. tragic/tragedy/tragic, heard, victims, refugees, headlines, van, Driver, shocked, blitz, worst, refused, coming, major, iconic, vivid, colorful, timeless, moments. Many cells in late layers point to “tragic”, “tragedy”, “iconic”, “vivid”, “headlines”, etc., which together suggest a pattern of phrasing used in news/incident reporting or attention-grabbing headlines.
- Coherence with layers: earlier layers show some other tokens (e.g. Sale/rock/cocktail) but these are low-norm relative to the late-layer/pos0 peaks; the dominant late-layer signals are the newsy/sensational tokens, which is what matters for final output preference.

Caveats / uncertainty
- Patchscope readouts were not provided, so I can’t verify the effect by seeing actual continuations when the difference is injected; that would be a strong confirmatory test.
- Some decoded tokens are noisy or mixed (e.g. “Sale”, punctuation, short fragments), so the pattern is not perfectly clean. The most consistent signal, however, is the set of headline/tragedy-related tokens in late layers.
- The evidence supports naming a topical/style difference (more “sensational/headline” language) but does not uniquely identify the training objective or mechanism that produced it.

Short answer: The difference looks like B (relative to A) induces a bias toward newsy/sensational / incident-report headline language at the start of generation, concentrated in late-layer, position-0 activations.
